blocks.text: el-buṭm). The press residues are called in Jewish Aramaic כוספא דבטמי [kwspʾ dbṭmy] (Hg. 58_{5. 29}).

Guigues p. XXXIX says: The green grains, granum viride (الحبّة الخضراء [al-ḥabba al-khaḍrāʾ]) of the Middle Ages, are the fruits of the terebinth, P. Tereb. L. They have been confused with pistachios, fusṭuḳ, fruits of P. vera L. Moreover, the green grains are still used as food today. It is above all in Mesopotamia that the fruits of the terebinth, buṭm, are edible.

בטנה [bṭnh], bŏṭnā,*) [Assyr. buṭnu, Zimmern AF. 54; Palmyr. בר בוטן [br bwṭn]**) n. pr. Chajes, Onomatolog. 12] also Mishnaic. Švi 7, 5: בוטנא [bwṭnʾ], variant reading בטנה [bṭnh] (TŠvi V 68_{14}, Schwarz p. 215), once also Targ. בוטנין [bwṭnyn] Gn. 43, 11.
boṭnā is a native tree, whereas pistachios are imported from abroad (j Dem. II 22^{b}_{69}). These come to Palestine from northern Syria (Rosen, Pf. 69).

The Mishnah and Tosefta passage cited speaks of young, edible shoots, לולב [lwlb]. The following are named: a) זרדים [zrdym], b) הרובים [hrwbym], c) אלה [ʾlh], d) בוטנה [bwṭnh], e) אטדין [ʾṭdyn], f) אדיל [ʾdyl]. c) according to Maimūnī, correctly, ballūṭ,***) i.e. ʾallā oak, not ʾēlā! Gal. VI 644 βλαστοὶ τερμίνθου [blastoi terminthou]! e) ῥάμνου [rhamnou]. He says: the terebinth shoots are pickled in vinegar or brine (Sachau, Inedita 95).

The place name bŏṭnā alone proves that the foreign pistachio cannot be meant. buṭm occurs as a place name in Arabic: Socin, Ortsapell. ZDPV. 22, 18: challet il-buṭm terebinth valley 31, 199, maḳāṭiʿ el-buṭmi terebinth quarry (31, 183).

בטנה [bṭnh] Jos. 13, 26, according to Robinson 3, 924 baṭne south of eṣ-ṣalt (Schwarz, Tebuot haareṣ ed. Luncz, p. 271 n). A place boṭnā also jAz. I 39^{d}_{27} = בטנן [bṭnn] B. r. 47 end. The fair at the terebinth ירידה של בוטנה [yrydh šl bwṭnh] (ZAW. 29, 217. 221). S. Klein has combined with this the market of בית האילם [byt hʾylm] MT. 185_{17} Hoffm., בית אילנים [byt ʾylnym] Sifre II 306, 132_{6} Friedm.

Dérenbourg has connected with the place name bŏtnā בטנית [bṭnyt] bŏṭnīt, a female proselyte from boṭnā (Sabb. 24, 5. Beza 3, 8. T. III 205_{27}. TMen XIII 533_{33}. [Pes. 57^{a}] Ned. 23^{a}. M. Zizit p. 23_{6} Kirchheim = Semaḥ. XII [p. 98_{12} Romm. for קטנים [qṭnym] read, with M. Zizit, Šibbŏlē 341 Buber and R. Elijah of Vilna, בטנית [bṭnyt]. ZAW. 29, 216).
On 1 K. 7, 20 מלעמת הבטן [mlʿmt hbṭn], F. Perles, neue Anal. 75, recalls boṭnīm.
S. Klein (I. 1926) refers to MS. 1910, 22 בית אילונים [byt ʾylwnym] for [בית] בטנה [[byt] bṭnh] and combines with it the name Abba Saul boṭnīt.
Flora 3, 254 is to be corrected accordingly.
